text: His being neither is exactly consistent with the probable feelings of a man spoilt in the common sense, but not really injured in disposition, and thoroughly in love. As for his being in love, Elizabeth has given as just an exposition of the causes of that phenomenon as Darcy has of the conditions of his unregenerate state, only she has of course not counted in what was due to her own personal charm. The secret of that charm many men and not a few women, from Miss Austen herself downwards, have felt, and like most charms it is a thing rather to be felt than to be explained.

The fog, a greasy, yellow visitation, clung to London as a shroud might to a corpse, and within its suffocating embrace, a disquiet settled upon the hearts of men – not a fear of thieves or debtors, though those anxieties were plentiful enough, but a colder, more insidious dread: the creeping suspicion that all endeavour was vanity, that the grand clockwork of society, for all its bustling and clamour, was wound by a careless hand and destined to run down into silence. Old Man Tiber, the lamplighter, confided in me, a man not given to philosophical musings, that the very flames he coaxed to life seemed to flicker with a mournful resignation, as if acknowledging the ultimate darkness. Even the costermongers’ cries lacked their usual robust cheer, replaced by a hollow echo that spoke of a world teetering on the precipice of meaninglessness, a precipice from which no amount of gin or good fortune could save us.

It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single fortune, though never so modest, must be the object of every young woman of good family; yet, it is a circumstance too often overlooked that the possession of such a competence does not invariably confer an equal degree of discernment, or indeed, of genuine worth. Miss Penrose, for instance, lately returned from a season in London, possessed a very comfortable income, and a wardrobe which, though not excessively brilliant, was undeniably fashionable. However, her conversation consisted chiefly of detailing the cut of a ballgown, or the precise shade of ribbon favoured by Lady Bellingham, matters of such profound consequence as to render any discussion of literature or morality quite superfluous. One could not but suspect that her mind, like a carefully arranged bouquet, was pleasing to the eye, but utterly devoid of fragrance.

It was an union that must have been to the advantage of both: by her ease and liveliness, his mind might have been softened, his manners improved; and from his judgment, information, and knowledge of the world, she must have received benefit of greater importance. But no such happy marriage could now teach the admiring multitude what connubial felicity really was. An union of a different tendency, and precluding the possibility of the other, was soon to be formed in their family. How Wickham and Lydia were to be supported in tolerable independence she could not imagine. But how little of permanent happiness could belong to a couple who were only brought together because their passions were stronger than their virtue, she could easily conjecture.

The assembly rooms at Meryton, though frequently the scene of much gaiety, offered, upon closer inspection, a rather disheartening spectacle of human vanity. Not that a degree of self-regard is wholly reprehensible; indeed, a modest confidence is essential to the proper conduct of life. But the eagerness with which young ladies catalogued each other’s gowns, and the breathless anticipation of a single approving glance from a gentleman of consequence, betrayed a shallowness of spirit that bordered on the ridiculous. Mrs. Philips, ever the keen observer of social currents, remarked to her daughters, with a knowing wink, that “a fine bonnet is half a husband already!” A sentiment, though uttered in jest, which spoke volumes regarding the prevailing standards of female worth within the neighbourhood.
